column2: The Puranas beginning with the Brahma, eighteen, are Hari's knowledge. In the great Agni Purana, Hari stands in the form of knowledge,
with creation and without creation, bearing the nature of the formed and the formless; having known him, worshipped and praised him, one would obtain enjoyment and liberation.
Vishnu, the victorious and the becoming, having the form of Agni, Sun and the rest; as Agni, Vishnu is the mouth of the gods and the supreme goal;
in the Vedas with the Puranas he is sung as the embodiment of sacrifice. The Purana named Agneya is the greater form of Vishnu.
The speaker and the hearer of the Agneya Purana is Janardana; therefore the Agni Purana is great, made of all the Vedas,
made of all knowledge, holy, made of all knowing, the best; the Self of all, the form of Hari, for men who recite and hear it;
for seekers of knowledge it gives knowledge; for seekers of wealth, prosperity and riches; for seekers of kingdom, kingdom; for those who wish dharma, dharma;
for seekers of heaven, heaven; for those desiring sons, sons; for those desiring cows and the like, cows; for those desiring a village, a village;
for those desiring desires, desires, giver of all good fortune; giver of virtue and fame to men; giver of victory to those desiring victory;
giver of all to those wishing all; giver of liberation to those wishing liberation; destroyer of sin for sinners — the Agneya Purana.
Where Narada told the dharmas based on the Brihat Kalpa, of twenty-five thousand verses, that is called the Naradiya;
one should give it with a cow in Ashvina and obtain final success. Where, regarding the enemies, there is deliberation on dharma and adharma,
the Markandeya of nine thousand, one should offer on the full moon of Kartika. What Agni told Vasishtha is the Agneya itself;
having written the book one should give it in Margashirsha; he is a giver of all. Twelve thousand only, enlightening all knowledge;
the Bhavishya of fourteen thousand, born of the Sun; Bhava told it to Manu; one should give it in Pausha with jaggery and the like.
The Brahmavaivarta was told by Savarni to Narada, the account of Rathantara, of eighteen thousand;
one should give the story of Varaha in Magha and share Brahma's world. Where Maheshvara, standing in the middle of the fire-linga, told the dharmas,
in the Agneya kalpa, that Linga of eleven thousand; having given it with a sesame cow in Phalguna one obtains Shiva.
The Varaha of fourteen thousand was told by Vishnu, the story of the Boar on earth through Manu's course;
with a golden Garuda in Chaitra one obtains Vishnu's station. The great Skanda of eighty-four thousand was told by Skanda;
concerning the dharmas in the Tatpurusha kalpa one should offer it. The Vamana of ten thousand, the story of Hari in the Dhauma kalpa,
one should give in autumn at the equinox, enlightening on dharma, wealth and the rest. The Kurma of eight thousand, told by Kurma in the netherworld,
in connection with Indradyumna, one should give with a golden tortoise. The Matsya of thirteen thousand told from the start of the kalpa;
Matsya gave it to Manu; one should give it at the equinox with a golden fish. The Garuda of eight thousand, told by Vishnu in the Tarkshya kalpa,
the birth of Garuda from the world-egg — one should give it with a golden swan. What Brahma told concerning the glory of the cosmic egg,
that, the Brahmanda of twelve thousand, one should offer to a Brahmin. In the Mahabharata at the end of each parva, with cloth, scents, garlands and the like,
one should first honor the reciter, feed Brahmins with pudding, and give cows, land, villages, gold and the like parva by parva.
At the end of the Mahabharata one should worship the Brahmin, the collections and books, having placed them in an auspicious place covered with silk cloth and the like;
Nara and Narayana are to be worshipped, and the books with flowers and the like; having given cows, food, land and gold, having fed, one should ask forgiveness.
Great gifts and various jewels should be given; two or three mashas each month one should have given.
At the solstice and the like, a gift to the reciter is ordained at the start; worship of the reciter should be done by all the listeners, twice-born.
One who gives books of the Itihasas and Puranas, having worshipped, obtains long life, health, heaven and liberation.
Manu had a daughter Ila; from Budha on her, Pururavas; having begotten Pururavas, Ila (Sela) attained the state of Sudyumna.
From Sudyumna came Utkala, Gaya and Vinatashva — three kings. Utkala's kingdom is Utkala; Vinatashva's the western
direction, all; Gaya's, of the best of kings, is Gayapuri. By Vasishtha's word Sudyumna obtained Pratishthana;
Sudyumna, having obtained the kingdom, gave it to Pururavas. Narishyanta's sons were the Shakas; Nabhaga's was Vaishnava;
Ambarisha, protector of subjects; from Dhrishta the Dharshtaka lineage. Sukalpa and Anarta of Sharyati; from Anarta, Vairohya the king;
the Anarta country and the city Kushasthali. Revata, son of Reva, named Kakudmi, righteous,
was eldest of a hundred sons; having obtained the kingdom at Kushasthali, with his daughter, having heard a Gandharva song near Brahma,
a moment for the god had passed many ages in the mortal world. He then came quickly to his own city filled with Yadavas,
made Dvaravati, of many gates, delightful, protected by Bhojas, Vrishnis and Andhakas, with Vasudeva at the front.
Knowing her blameless, he gave Revati to Baladeva. Having performed austerity on the peak of Sumeru, he went to Vishnu's abode.
Two sons of Nabhaga, Vaishyas, became Brahmins; from Karusha the Karushas, Kshatriyas, mad in battle;
Prishadhra went to Shudrahood after killing his teacher's cow. From Manu's son Ikshvaku, Vikukshi became the king of gods (Shashada);
of Vikukshi was Kakutstha; his son Suyodhana; his son named Prithu; Vishvagashva, son of Prithu;
his son Ayu; then Yuvanashva a son; from Yuvanashva Shravanta, in the east the city Shravanti;
from Shravanta Brihadashva; then the king Kuvalashva, who of old attained the name Dhundhumara from Dhundhu.
Three Dhundhumara kings: Dridhashva and Danda; Kapila; from Dridhashva Haryashva and Pramodaka;
from Haryashva Nikumbha; Samhatashva from Nikumbha; Akrishashva and Ranashva, both sons of Samhatashva;
Yuvanashva of Ranashva; Mandhata from Yuvanashva; of Mandhata Purukutsa; Muchukunda the second;
from Purukutsa Trasadasyu, born of Narmada; of Sambhuta Sudhanva; then Tridhanva from Sudhanva;
of Tridhanva Taruna; his son Satyavrata; from Satyavrata Satyaratha, and Harishchandra his son;
from Harishchandra Rohitashva; from Rohitashva Vrika; from Vrika Bahu; and of Bahu Sagara, with his beloved,
Prabha, who became the mother of sixty thousand sons. By the pleased sage Aurva one son Asamanjasa of Bhanumati;
the diggers of the earth were burned by Vishnu, with many oceans. Asamanjasa, Amshuman, and Dilipa of Amshuman;
Bhagiratha from Dilipa, by whom the Ganga was brought down; from Bhagiratha Nabhaga; from Nabhaga Ambarisha;
Sindhudvipa from Ambarisha; his son is remembered Shrutayu; from Shrutayu Ritaparna; his Kalmashapada;
from Kalmashapada Sarvakarma; then Anaranya; from Anaranya Nighna, then Anamitra, then Raghu;
of Raghu Dilipa, and from Dilipa king Aja; Dirghabahu from Aja; Kala; then Ajapala;
then Dasharatha was born, with four sons, all of Narayana's nature; Rama was his eldest.
The king, best of Raghus, killer of Ravana in Ayodhya, whose deeds Valmiki composed having heard from Narada.
Rama's sons, Kusha and Lava, born of Sita, increasers of the line; Atithi was born of Kusha; Nishadha his son.
From Nishadha Nala was born; from Nala Nabha was born; from Nabha Pundarika; then Sudhanva;
from Sudhanva Devanika, and Ahinashva his son; from Ahinashva Sahasrashva; then Chandraloka;
from Chandravaloka Tarapida; from him Chandraparvata; from Chandragiri Bhanuratha; Shrutayu his son. Those born of the Ikshvaku line are remembered as bearers of the Solar dynasty.
Dyuti left Vibhavasu, Pushti the imperishable Dhatri; Prabha left Prabhakara, Kuhu herself left Havishmat;
Kirti left her husband Jayanta, Vasu left Marichi-Kashyapa; Dhriti left her husband Nandi; then they resorted to Soma alone.
Soma too, as if they were his own, desired them then. Thus for him who had done the wrong, the hosts of their husbands then
could not retaliate by curses and weapons. He, having attained sole lordship of the seven worlds by austerity,
his mind wandered, struck by lack of humility. He seized Brihaspati's wife, the glorious Tara by name,
by force, Soma, having slighted Angiras' son. Then the famous war, Tarakamaya, took place,
of gods and demons, a great destroyer of the worlds. Brahma, having prevented Ushanas, gave Tara to Angiras.
Seeing her pregnant, the teacher said, "Abandon the child." The embryo, abandoned, blazing, then said, "I am born of Soma."
Thus from Soma Budha was the son; his son Pururavas. The Apsara Urvashi, leaving heaven, chose him.
The king lived with her for ten and five years, five, six, seven, eight, ten and eight, great sage.
